title: Appsmith Pricing 2026: Plans, Costs and Limits
summary: Appsmith pricing includes free entry, business plans at $15 per user, and enterprise options metered by user count.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


### Is Appsmith really free?


Yes, up to a point: the hosted cloud product has a free plan, and it covers a small team's first build. The catch is that the limit is on how many people can use the app.


Once real users arrive, you hit that ceiling, and the paid tier has the extra seats and some features. Check the pricing page for the current user cap before you build, not after.


### Does self-hosting Appsmith cost anything?


You can run the software itself on your own servers without a license fee, but "free" stops there. You pay for the machine it runs on, and someone has to handle upgrades, backups and uptime.


Even when you host it yourself, some parts of the product are paid-only, so confirm which ones your app needs. If your app depends on one, self-hosting doesn't avoid the paid tier.


### Can you pay for Appsmith annually and save money?


Vendors in this category commonly discount annual billing against monthly, and it's worth asking whether Appsmith's paid plan does. I wouldn't lean on that to make a build pencil out.


Because the unit that drives your bill is the number of users, annual billing only lowers the rate on a headcount you may not have settled. Settle the user count first, then compare monthly and annual for that number.


### What happens when you go over a plan's limit?


It depends on which limit you cross. A user cap generally means new people can't be added until you move to a higher plan. A feature that sits behind the paid tier simply isn't available to you until you upgrade.


In both cases the cost shows up when you roll the app out, which is why the limit matters more than the sticker price. Read the plan terms for exactly what's blocked and what's billed.


### Is Appsmith cheaper than Retool?


It can be, but the comparison only holds on one workload. Retool, another tool for building internal apps, is also priced by user, and its plan decides what you can use.


So price both against the same app: the same number of editors, the same number of end users, and the same must-have features.


Whichever tool needs the paid tier for fewer of those will cost less. A headline per-user rate by itself won't tell you which one that's.
